title: Everywhere
hookLine: Jewish communities in Argentina, Canada, Australia, South Africa and beyond

lines: THEN CAPE TOWN, BUENOS AIRES, TORONTO.
A LINE OF CANDLES AROUND THE WORLD.
cards: Friday evening reaches Melbourne while much of the world is still at work. Candles are lit, a blessing is sung over wine, and Shabbat begins. Hours later the sun sets over Cape Town, and it happens again.
Then Buenos Aires. Then Toronto. As the evening rolls around the globe, the same small table scene keeps lighting up, city after city, in English, Spanish and Hebrew, in every kind of accent.
Today, that whole moving line of candles. Today's word is Everywhere.

teach.b: The great wave didn't only flow to New York. Families leaving Eastern Europe looked for any door that would open.

In Argentina, some settled in Jewish farming colonies out on the plains, and their riders came to be called Jewish gauchos. Others settled in Buenos Aires. In Canada, families settled in Montreal, Toronto and Winnipeg.
In South Africa, Jews from Lithuania were among those who arrived, and built synagogues from Johannesburg to Cape Town. In Australia, Jewish communities grew in Melbourne and Sydney.
And there are more: Mexico, Brazil, Britain, France, places this path has already visited and places it hasn't. How do you live in so many places at once and stay one people?

teach.h: FROM THE RISING OF THE SUN.
teach.b: A line from the Psalms, sung in the Hallel on festivals, gives one picture of it: "From the rising of the sun unto the going down thereof the LORD'S name is to be praised."
Read on a globe, that line is a chain of candles.
When the sun goes down in one city, it is still up in the next, and the praise passes along.
So Jewish communities became part of each place: speaking its language, cheering its teams, serving in its schools and hospitals.

In some synagogues a prayer for the country and its leaders is said in the service, each place in its own words. And at the same time, the same Torah is read, the same Shabbat begins, the same holidays come round.
Everywhere doesn't mean nowhere. It means rooted in each city, and passing the same evening along to all the others.

how: Jewish communities around the world keep the same Shabbat and holidays in their own languages and accents, and in some synagogues a prayer for the welfare of the country is said during the service.

o: Jews with no country, living nowhere in particular
a rule that Shabbat starts at one hour worldwide
Jewish communities rooted in cities across the world

p: riders of farming colonies in Argentina
said in some synagogues, in local words

s: the great wave went only to New York
families went to Argentina, Canada, South Africa, Australia and beyond.
the psalm praises from the rising of the sun to its going down
"from the rising of the sun unto the going down thereof the LORD'S name is to be praised."
living everywhere means a community belongs nowhere
rooted in each city, and connected to all the others by the same Torah, Shabbat and holidays.

games.q: it is Friday evening in Melbourne, and the Shabbat candles are lit. where are people still waiting for sunset?
o: nowhere; Shabbat starts everywhere at once.
Cape Town, Buenos Aires and Toronto, still waiting for sunset.
games.why: Shabbat begins at each city's own sunset, so the candles light up one city after another around the globe.

practice: Choose one place from today, Buenos Aires, Toronto, Winnipeg, Melbourne or Cape Town, and hold it in mind: somewhere there, right now, people are cooking, studying, praying.
Then turn to your own city, and wish both places peace, in your own words, or, if you pray, with the words you already know.

wordCard.voice: Everywhere. Jewish communities in Argentina, Canada, Australia, South Africa and beyond, each rooted in its own city, all keeping the same Shabbat. Today's word.
